notes:
I've written verse-by-verse notes on Habakkuk 1 below. The older commentaries and Enduring Word gave the best coverage. Some things are missing:
- **Not found:** anything from bibleodyssey.org, the NET Bible notes themselves, Orthodox sources (oca.org), Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Wesleyan sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace writers. I ran out of searches.
- **Lutheran:** Luther appears only where Keil quotes him.
- **Methodist:** I used Adam Clarke instead.
- **NET:** only its translation wording appears.
- **Thin coverage:** vv. 9–11 and 14–17 have less than the other verses.
- **Not true schools of thought:** each tradition is represented by one or two of its own commentators.
- **Links without a citation tag:** I read Barnes' whole chapter on one StudyLight page. Those points just carry the URL.

---

**v. 1**
- **"Burden":** Guzik says it means both a message from God and a heavy weight, because it announced judgment on Judah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/ Gill adds that it was hard news for the Jews: the Chaldeans would invade and take them captive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/1-1.htm
- **Date:** Guzik says we can't be sure. His estimate is between Babylon's conquest of Nineveh (612 BC) and of Jerusalem (587 BC). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/
- **"The prophet":** Guzik quotes Baker that this rare title may mean Habakkuk was a professional prophet at the Temple or court. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/
- **The name:** Barnes says it means "strong embrace", which suits a book about faith holding on to God when things don't make sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/habakkuk-1.html

**v. 2**
- **Whose violence?** Guzik says Habakkuk saw violence and injustice in Judah and wondered why God didn't put it right. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/
- **Why it's Judah:** Barnes argues the words describe strife among neighbours, not a foreign enemy. Habakkuk is listing Judah's own sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/habakkuk-1.html
- **Grieving for others:** Matthew Henry notes Habakkuk hadn't been wronged himself. It grieved him to see others wronged. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hab/Hab_001.cfm

**v. 3**
- **Seeing sin in yourself:** Spurgeon preached on this verse. He said God shows us our own sin so that He can rescue us from it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_habakkuk
- **Seeing sin in others:** Spurgeon also said God shows us others' sin so we will work harder to save souls. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_habakkuk Guzik takes up the same two reasons. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/
- **Calvin (Reformed):** reading these sins as the Chaldeans' is "strained". Habakkuk is grieving over evil among God's own chosen people. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom29/cache/calcom29.html3
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** the same words are later used of the Chaldeans. Judah sinned by violence and would be punished by violence. They link this to the injustice of King Jehoiakim's reign. https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB35.htm

**v. 4**
- **Paralysed law:** Precept Austin prefers the NIV's "paralyzed". Corrupt leaders made the law ineffective. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60383/
- **Barnes:** the Hebrew literally says the law is "chilled", for lack of love. He links this to Matthew 24:12, where love grows cold. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/habakkuk-1.html
- **Guzik:** Habakkuk saw sin everywhere, from personal relationships to the courts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/

**v. 5**
- **"Too bad to be true":** Guzik says this isn't something too good to believe. It is judgment too terrible to believe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/
- **Paul's use in Acts 13:40–41:** Precept Austin says Paul turns this into a warning against rejecting the gospel. That fate would be worse than any Babylonian invasion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_1_commentary
- **Henry:** the fall of Jerusalem to the Chaldeans was a picture of its later fall to Rome. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hab/Hab_001.cfm Calvin says the same: Paul applied this vengeance to Jews who rejected Christ. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom29/cache/calcom29.html3
- **Wording:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that Paul's "wonder and perish" gives the meaning, not the exact Hebrew wording. https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB35.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock says Paul follows the Greek Old Testament's "ye despisers". He calls Paul's reading the "mystical sense" and the literal sense "very obscure". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/habakkuk-1.html

**v. 6**
- **God and the Chaldeans' sin:** Guzik says the Babylonians came as sent by the LORD. Their own sinful wish to conquer was allowed to succeed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/
- **Henry:** Judah stirred up strife among themselves, so God would stir up the Chaldeans against them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hab/Hab_001.cfm
- **Calvin:** the Chaldeans came moved by God's hidden impulse, not just their own instinct. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom29/cache/calcom29.html3
- **Barnes:** God uses people's free will and evil passions for His own ends. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/habakkuk-1.html

**v. 7**
- **Their own law:** Calvin says the Chaldeans would be their own judges. Their power would serve as their law and their sword as their court. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom29/cache/calcom29.html3
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** they recognise no judge but themselves. https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB35.htm
- **Barnes:** this lawless self-exaltation is "a character of antichrist" (Daniel 11:36; 2 Thessalonians 2:4). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/habakkuk-1.html

**v. 8**
- **Animal pictures:** Barnes says the "leopard" is the panther, the swiftest and fiercest beast of prey. "Evening wolves" are wolves made fiercest by a day of hunger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/habakkuk-1.html Spurgeon made the same point about the evening wolf. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_habakkuk
- **Calvin:** the eagle picture means the Chaldeans would swoop instantly on any prey. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom29/cache/calcom29.html3

**v. 9**
- **"East wind":** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown take it as the simoon, the scorching desert wind. Its whirlwinds of sand fit "gathering captives like sand". They reject reading it as "eastward". https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB35.htm
- **Catholic:** the Knox Bible note on New Advent says the Hebrew here is obscure. It may mean "faces set eastward" or simply "forward". https://www.newadvent.org/bible/hab001.htm

**v. 10**
- **Calvin:** the Chaldeans would not fight an uncertain war but simply triumph. Judah's alliance with Egypt and its pride were false hopes. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom29/cache/calcom29.html3
- **Criswell (quoted on Precept Austin):** no fortress is too high, because they quickly build earth mounds to climb over it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_1_commentary

**v. 11**
- **Credit to false gods:** Guzik says the Babylonians would wrongly give the credit to their false gods, and God knew this beforehand. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/
- **Henry:** names Bel and Nebo as the gods who got the credit. He warns that taking God's glory is the "common offence of proud people". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hab/Hab_001.cfm
- **Criswell:** proud of their wins, they made a god of their own power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_1_commentary
- **Calvin** (on the KJV's "his mind will change"): success went to their heads. God would punish that arrogance, which gives the faithful hope. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom29/cache/calcom29.html3
- **Catholic:** Haydock links the verse to Nebuchadnezzar's humbling in Daniel 4 and the quick fall of the empire. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/habakkuk-1.html The Knox note says the Hebrew gives a doubtful sense and may be corrupt. https://www.newadvent.org/bible/hab001.htm

**v. 12**
- **Traditional reading:** Precept Austin says the opening question is rhetorical and expects "Yes". When confused, Habakkuk goes back to what he knows about God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_1_commentary
- **Henry:** God is from everlasting, so the church will last. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hab/Hab_001.cfm

*Where traditions differ on "we will not die":*
- **Reformed:** Calvin says it means the nation would not be destroyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/1-12.html
- **Methodist/Arminian:** Clarke says Judah would "not be totally exterminated". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/1-12.html
- **Calvinist Baptist:** Gill says it means neither bodily death nor affliction but spiritual death, from which none of God's people will perish. He ties this to everlasting election and covenant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/1-12.htm
- **Precept Austin:** applies it to believers in Christ: they may die physically but will not suffer the second, eternal death. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_1_commentary
- **Lutheran (Luther, quoted by Keil):** the question form shows how faith survives conflict. Faith stands firm, yet it "cracks" and sounds different mid-battle than after victory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/1-12.htm

*Text and scholarship:*
- **"Correction of the scribes":** Jewish tradition counts "we will not die" among 18 scribal corrections. The original is said to be "You will not die". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/1-12.htm
- **Keil's explanation:** these aren't later changes to the text. The prophet meant "You will not die" but reworded it out of reverence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/1-12.htm
- **Translations:** the NIV reads "you will never die" and the NET "you are immortal". https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/1-12.htm
- **Other readings:** Benson notes Secker's rendering "Let us not die". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/1-12.htm Clarke reports Houbigant's emendation "God of truth". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/1-12.html
- **"Appointed them for judgment":** Ewald held that it is the Chaldeans who are appointed *to be* judged. The Cambridge commentary calls this "less natural". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/1-12.htm The Catholic Knox note likewise says it isn't clear which is meant. https://www.newadvent.org/bible/hab001.htm

**v. 13**
- **Guzik:** Habakkuk knew God was holy, so he was more troubled that God would exalt even more wicked Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/
- **Barnes:** God's hatred of evil is pictured as being unable to look at it, the way a person turns from a sickening sight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/habakkuk-1.html
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "those who deal treacherously" are the Chaldeans, once Judah's allies. Judah, for all its faults, was better than its oppressor. https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB35.htm
- **Henry:** many Jews were as bad as the Chaldeans, but some were far more righteous and were still devoured. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hab/Hab_001.cfm

*Popular teaching debated:*
- **Chuck Smith:** reads "behold" as behold with approval. He then links the verse to God forsaking His Son when the world's sins were laid on Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/1-13.html
- **GotQuestions pushes back on the popular idea:** the verse doesn't mean God has to shut His eyes or turn His back on sin. In the poetry, "look on" parallels "tolerate", so it means God won't approve of sin. https://www.gotquestions.org/God-look-upon-sin.html

**v. 14**
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** like fish anyone can catch, God's people have lost their defender. It is as if there were no God. https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB35.htm
- **ESV Study Bible (quoted on Precept Austin):** Habakkuk charges that God lets people act like lower creatures with no ruler, so wickedness goes unchecked. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60383/

**v. 15**
- **Henry:** the oppressors thought no more of killing people than of catching fish. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hab/Hab_001.cfm
- **Guzik:** God's people were conquered as easily as fish caught in a net. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/

**v. 16**
- **Precept Austin:** the sacrifices to the net describe Babylon worshipping the "gods" of power and violence. It quotes Ronald Blue: idolatry isn't limited to burning incense to objects. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60383/

**v. 17**
- **Precept Austin:** Habakkuk expected "No" to this question. God would step in, in His time, and deal justly with the Chaldeans. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_1_commentary
- **Guzik:** Habakkuk wondered how long the cruel conquest would go on. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-1/

---

**Catholic background on dating (whole chapter)**
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** prefers a date of 605–600 BC. It calls v. 5 an incredible prediction at the time, since Judah was God's kingdom. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/07097a.htm
- **Knox note:** in contrast, suggests vv. 5–11 may describe events that had already happened. It says Habakkuk may have lived during the captivity (Daniel 14). https://www.newadvent.org/bible/hab001.htm
- **Haydock disagrees with itself:** its introduction gives the general view that he is the Habakkuk of Daniel 14. Its v. 6 note says the Chaldeans weren't yet that great, so he can't be. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/habakkuk/1.htm
